newsitem.title: FRANCE: Poll shows French more Gaullist, more opinionated.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows French more Gaullist, more opinionated.

text.p: Charles de Gaulle has been dead for a quarter of a century but Gaullism -- the belief in national independence for France -- is stronger than when he was alive, according to an opinion poll released on Thursday.

The Louis Harris poll, an unusual one in the flurry of surveys pouring out every week from polling institutes, put to voters the same questions they were asked in 1966, the year de Gaulle pulled France out of NATO's military wing.
It showed the percentage of voters favouring de Gaulle's concerns with diplomatic and military independence had shot up.
But the clearest conclusion of the survey of 1,003 voters was that the French had become much more opinionated. On all issues, the percentage of "don't knows" fell dramatically.
An overwhelming 84 percent majority said they wanted France's foreign policy to be independent from the United States, up from 54 percent in 1966.

The percentage of voters wanting France to have its own nuclear strike force -- de Gaulle's brainchild -- rose to 63 from 31 percent, and those favouring powerful armed forces rose to 53 from 48 percent.

Gaullist President Jacques Chirac plans to switch to an all-professional army without conscripts by 2002 and to take France back into the NATO fold. Earlier this year, he ended controversial nuclear tests to upgrade the nuclear arsenal.

Despite current disaffection with the European Union, the poll showed the French to be more pro-European, with the percentage of those favouring a halt in the construction of Europe falling to 48 percent from 63 percent.
Other questions showed French voters to be more decidedly in favour of aiding the Third World and maintaining state financing of private schools.

On some issues they appeared confused. The percentage of both yes and no answers grew when voters were asked if they favoured socialism, wanted to curtail the right to strike in public services or wanted to privatise state companies.

The poll also asked voters a variety of new questions. It showed that two thirds were opposed to decriminalising consumption of soft drugs and 82 percent wanted to cut working hours to fight record unemployment.

Two thirds favoured making it more difficult to acquire French citizenship in order to curb immigration, and 56 percent to 37 percent opposed banning the far-right National Front which espouses racist ideas and campaigns to send immigrants home.
A narrow majority favoured stiffening conditions for the destitute to be given state financial aid.
